extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in natural history, animal domestication, heredity, and Victorian-era scientific discussion
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the conditions and practical principles under which wild animals may become domesticated, together with related principles of selection, breeding, and human influence on races. Includes illustrative examples and limits of selective breeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardiness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed in the author's final summary as the first essential condition for domestication; implies the animal must withstand confinement, handling, and changes of environment that accompany association with humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inborn liking for man
rubrics_metrics.description: They should have an inborn liking for man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explains that animals with an instinctive affinity for humans are more likely to be kept and bred (examples: affectionate seals; goats that readily let children suckle). Lack of this affinity makes permanent domestication unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comfort‑loving disposition
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comfort‑loving animals prefer the comforts of human habitations and are less inclined to revert to the wild; contrast with animals that 'thoroughly enjoy the excitement of wild life' which 'cannot be domesticated' (they may only be tamed). The cat is cited as a comfort‑loving exception despite being non‑gregarious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness to man
rubrics_metrics.description: They should be found useful to the savages (useful to man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility (food, milk, barter value, status) motivates people to protect and breed animals. Examples: the role of milk (goats) for children, seals that were tolerated only because of affectionate ways but would have been more widely kept if useful; menageries established from chiefs' pleasure. The author notes that utility as a food store is the most durable motive for maintaining animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breed freely under confinement
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A crucial limiting condition: species that will not reproduce in captivity cannot be domesticated. Examples: North American turkey allegedly unknown in the third generation in captivity; turtles placed in lagoons by Upper Amazon Indians which could have become domesticated if they bred in captivity. The author emphasizes this as 'one of the most important' conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easy to tend (gregariousness/controlability)
rubrics_metrics.description: They should be easy to tend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential that large numbers be controllable by few herdsmen; gregariousness is a key quality (herds stay together and are easier to manage). Non‑gregarious species are hard to maintain (described as 'like a falling necklace of beads whose string is broken'). The cat is an exception retained because of adhesion to household comforts despite non‑gregariousness. Includes anecdote from Australian natives showing dogs sometimes leave masters when food is scarce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aversion to permanent wild freedom (cannot thoroughly enjoy wild life)
rubrics_metrics.description: If animals thoroughly enjoy the excitement of wild life they cannot be domesticated; they could only be tamed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author contrasts animals that, after tasting the wilderness, will not return (thus only tamed) versus those that are content in captivity. This is given as a disqualifying characteristic for domestication (anti‑pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on man for protection/use reduces reversion to wildness
rubrics_metrics.description: Species not dependent on man for protection are more likely to revert to wildness (example: elephants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, powerful animals (elephants) that do not need human protection often revert to wildness if given opportunity; cost and comparative uselessness also deter domestication. Recounted observations about captured elephants reverting or being kept imprisoned briefly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of tamest for breeding (artificial selection process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tame individuals that keep the flock together and are less likely to run away are preserved and become parents; the tamest become progenitors of the domestic herd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author describes continual, often unconscious selection by humans: wilder animals are slaughtered when necessary and tamer animals are saved, leading over generations to domestic aptitudes becoming established. He cites witnessing this among pastoral savages in South Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions and contextual constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Some species may appear exceptions due to special circumstances (e.g., African elephant, North American reindeer, certain ducks/geese), but these do not overturn the general conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author enumerates apparent exceptions and explains why they are not strong counterexamples (e.g., nomadic habits limit retention of aquatic birds). Use these examples to test the robustness of the domesticability criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of intense selective breeding (delicacy and infertility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overbreeding for particular qualities leads to increased delicacy of constitution, diminished fertility, and sexual indifference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as fundamental constraints on the extent to which selection can improve a race: highly-bred animals often become fragile and less fertile (examples: 'weedy' colts, horses and dogs showing sexual indifference). This warns against expecting indefinite improvement through selection alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish individual excellence from race quality
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual's high qualities may be exceptional within a poor race or average in a high one; the distinction is revealed by the descendants' reversion toward the race's typical centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consideration for selection: permanent improvement requires a change in the race's typical centre (emergence of a new typical centre), otherwise stringent selection yields only temporary gains that revert when selection is relaxed. Use pedigree/descendant behaviour to infer whether excellence is race‑level or individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of superior strains for propagation (human eugenics stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Superior strains are identifiable by strong family resemblances, prepotency over spouses in offspring, and being as prolific as their class; such strains can be favored so their progeny outnumber and replace older stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author suggests (as a policy idea) that the 'most merciful form of what I ventured to call "eugenics" ' would favor superior strains that are both prepotent and sufficiently prolific. He recommends studying such strains (e.g., families of exiles) as they are convenient to trace and may supply new strains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human social processes that alter racial composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence of man upon race occurs via migrations, invasions, war, deportation, emigration, and social customs (e.g., marriage patterns) which have a silent but widespread effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate or predict racial change, consider these human processes; the author discusses examples (Spain's layered invasions, colonization patterns, immigration effects in the Americas and Oceania) and notes that mixture and replacement can proceed 'silently and slowly' through differential fertility, marriage, and economic advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical caution: distinguish race vs individual and avoid a priori moral judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Our ignorance of criteria distinguishing races/sub‑races and the complex historical admixtures counsel caution; observational evidence should guide conclusions rather than purely deductive moral arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author warns about misleading terms like 'aborigines' and emphasizes the complexity of population histories; when evaluating racial differences or replacement, appeal to observation and historical/archaeological/linguistic evidence rather than simplistic a priori reasoning.
